div.font: Appendix D (4/5)
Purpose, Explanation, and Arbitrariness

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 796px; height: 1px; padding-top: 473px; margin-left: 28px;

span.b: 6. "Randomness (and/or the laws of physics) better explain reality than God."

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); text-align: left;
background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 12px;

div.font: - "The God-of-the-Gaps fallacy (ie. argument from ignorance): the more we know about reality and science, the less 'God' is required to explain it."
- "The universe could just be an emergent result of quantum fluctuations - this explains the universe just as well as (or even better than) God does."
- "Reality" can be rationally understood without appealing to God (ie. some transcendent, conscious creator) for the answer.
- The laws of physics explain reality just as well as God does - or even better, actually, because physics is testable and falsifiable, while God is not.
- An alternate explanation for reality equally (or with a better fit) explains reality.

font.b: How the Project Addresses These Commitments

div.font: - "An alternate explanation for reality equally (or better) explains reality" and "the more we know about reality, the less 'God' is required to explain it".

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - Firstly, the "laws of physics" are simply patterns in reality that we observe to occur without exception - and they are only meaningful within their context.

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - Ex. Apples fall down, every time we try - except if its speed is greater than some value, in which it will either orbit or move away from the Earth. So, the inferred "law" is that "objects follow the path of some force (or forced path) we'll call gravity".

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - As such, the subject of investigation would shift from "what causes apples to fall?" to "what causes gravity to function?", and neither of these arrive at a "fundamental cause" - which is what "God" claims to explain.

div.font: - Secondly, we did not derive our definition of "God" by looking at what we don't know - rather, we deduced God's definition from the inferences we do know. In other words, we didn't say, "we don't know ____, so it must be God" - rather, this project deduces, "God must be ____ because of ____ observation". And those deductions come from inferences that encompass all reality - just like laws of physics are inferred to encompass all reality.
- As such, the "God" explanation is not only meaningful for explaining what we don't know, but - more importantly - what we do know.

- Ex. Newton looks up in the sky and observes how the planets move according to God's plan/will. He discovers that they move predictably according to gravity, but doesn't know why their orbits have these strange variations that gravity doesn't explain. He deduces that God must be inserting those variations somehow - but note that this deduction does not eliminate the original claim: that the planets move according to God's plan/will.
- So, as "God" is claimed to be the fundamental cause/explanation of all things, any "law of reality" we observe is simply a discovery of how it manifests.

- As a result, to argue that "science explains reality as equally (or better than) God does" is to make a category error: if the "God" claim is understood properly, then all sciences and inferred laws are merely observed manifestations of God's will - meaning that "God" always explains reality at a higher level than any "law of reality" can explain.

- It's like saying "'falling down' explains the path of an apple just as well as 'gravity' does", which would be incorrect: they are at different levels of explanation (each within their own context) with the "gravity" explanation encompassing the "falling down" explanation - not contradicting it.
- So, if you reject the concept that God encompasses all laws of reality, then you either (see the Cost of Disagreement section for each):

font.b: - Reject that laws are fundamentally inferred, not derived.
- Reject the inferences that were made from reality.
- Reject how "God" is derived from those inferences.

div.font: - Any variation of "quantum mechanics explains the fundamental cause of reality, so God isn't necessary

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.font: - The fundamental behavior of quantum mechanics is decided by the "collapse of the wave function", by which there are two possibilities (and neither are confirmed, as both equally describe the data - see Appendix E): its randomness is truly fundamental (ie. it's indeterministic, lacking cause-and-effect - like the project's derivation of "will") or is a veil over some deeper behavior (ie. it's deterministic, possessing cause-and-effect - but we simply don't know how).

- Notably, both interpretations fit the "God" explanation as the mechanism/manifestation for God's will: if quantum behavior is indeterministic, then it would be fundamentally how God's will manifests into reality - and if it's deterministic, then quantum mechanics has still not reached the level of fundamental explanation.
- So, the "God" explanation still encompasses both cases - meaning that quantum mechanics does not explain reality at an equal or higher level.
- So, the claim

span.style: background-color: transparent; font-size: 11px; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: that "quantum mechanics is a better explanation than God" is no different than the "laws of physics" argument - and because the fundamental behavior of the quantum wave function is currently unknown, to make an argument either way would be making a reverse argument from ignorance - using what we don't know to declare a metaphysical conclusion.

span.b: 5. "This whole process is arbitrary: you chose the rules that conveniently lead to your conclusion."

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); text-align: left;
background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 12px;

div.font: - "You picked this process because you like it/it leads to the conclusion you want."
- "Other epistemologies are equally valid."
- This project lacks integrity, arbitrarily cherry-picking a set of rules and observations - hiding what is essentially whim/preference.
- There are so many other approaches to truth, and this particular one was chosen just to make it seem like the conclusion is valid - when others wouldn't agree.

- Either:
- This project implements double standards - as in, the rules it derives are only selectively applied.
- All epistemologies (ie. approaches to truth) are equally valid.
- Another epistemology is better than this, and - out of the project's lack of integrity - has been omitted from the analysis.

font.b: How the Project Addresses These Commitments

div.font: - "This project applies double standards

span.style: background-color: transparent; font-size: 11px; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: " or "another epistemology is better than this".

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - This will have to be proven (ie. identifying the double standard or better alternative) - otherwise, the claim reduces to "I don't agree, so it must be wrong".

div.font: - "All epistemologies are equally valid".
- This claim depends on the definition for "valid":

- If "valid" means "[logically] consistent", then that is precisely the same condition this project aims to uphold - and if that condition is challenged by this claim, then this claim is actually a double standard (ie. critiquing the project's rule for consistency, yet selectively allowing it for this claim).

- If "valid" means "sufficient", "meaningful", or some form of "it just is" (ie. the feeling of "good enough"), then see the "Reality doesn't need purpose/will to explain its behavior" section - as well as the Cost of Disagreement section in the conclusion.

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

font.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.font: f you reject the project's implementation of consistency, it requires proof.
